title: Mastering Lamellar Keratoplasty: DALK vs DMEK vs DSAEK

branches: DALK: Keratoconus, Corneal Scars, Corneal Dystrophies (Anterior)
DSAEK: Fuchs' Dystrophy, Bullous Keratopathy, ICE Syndrome
DMEK: Fuchs' Dystrophy, Failed DSAEK, Posterior Polymorphous Dystrophy

sections.title: Key Advantages of Each Technique
content: DALK: Eliminates endothelial rejection risk and maintains the integrity of the host's inner cornea.
DSAEK: Technically easier graft handling than DMEK; automated microtome creates predictable graft thickness.
DMEK: Superior visual acuity (often 20/20 or 20/25); minimal stromal interface interference.
Both Endothelial (DMEK/DSAEK): Small incision surgery, no suture-related astigmatism, rapid recovery compared to PKP.

sections.title: Critical Red Flags & Complications
content: Graft Detachment (High risk in DMEK, requires re-bubbling)
Pupillary Block Glaucoma (from air/gas bubble migration)
Interface Haze or Scarring (Specific to DALK and DSAEK)
Inadvertent Descemet's Membrane Perforation (During DALK dissection)
Primary Graft Failure (Non-clearing cornea within 4 weeks)

sections.title: Note on Technical Execution
sections.content: Lamellar surgery represents a paradigm shift from full-thickness Penetrating Keratoplasty (PKP). DALK focuses on stromal replacement while sparing the healthy endothelium. In contrast, DSAEK and DMEK focus solely on the posterior layers, replacing the diseased endothelium while preserving the anterior structure of the host cornea. Choice of procedure depends on the patient's specific layer of disease and the surgeon's expertise with ultrathin tissues.
